scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Named after the zonari or belt that dancers hold, this open-circle dance anchored displaced communities across Evros following the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne.
This is Zonaradiko. 1920s (modern documented form).

Title card: Zonaradiko · Greece · 1920s (modern documented form)

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Zonaradiko originated in the Thrace region spanning northern Greece and neighbouring territories.

Following the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923, refugee populations—including Cappadocians, Pontic Greeks, and Thracians from Bulgaria and Turkey—settled heavily in northern Evros, where the dance emerged as an identity marker across these distinct groups.
The movement sequence corresponds directly to the Bulgarian Pravo Trakijsko Horo.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed as a social village dance across Greek and Bulgarian Thrace, Zonaradiko served as a vital cultural binder for indigenous residents and resettled refugee groups in northern Evros after 1923.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers stand in an open circle or line with knees bent throughout the dance, holding the waist belts (zonaria) of adjacent dancers with the leader on the far right.
The basic structure consists of 12 counts containing 8 steps.
In western Thrace variants, the line leads into a spiral around the leader before untwisting.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Zonaradiko is danced to traditional Thracian folk melodies.

narration: The dance is traditionally performed in open-circle formations at village gatherings throughout Thrace.
A crucial element of the attire is the zonari (cloth belt or sash) worn around the waist, which provides the handhold for the line.

narration: No individual historical choreographers or historical soloists are detailed in the sources.
In northern Thrace, Zonaradiko shifts into a fast phase known as tsestos.
Directly related to the broader Balkan family of Pravo line dances found across Bulgaria and Greece.

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Zonaradiko (Greece). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
